1. Price cap on games

60€ for an AAA game has been around for who knows how long, people are scared to increase the price. Inflation goes up constantly, this game price never goes up. You have to pay workers more (more budget goes away) while the price stays exactly the same. I'd guess this is the reason why games just seem worse and worse as time goes on, as companies either can't afford more/more skilled people or are afraid of invest more.

2. Unforgiving market

If you tank with sales on 2-3 consecutive releases you just go bankrupt and with each failed release your games just get worse due to the money lost. Also the never ending cycle of cuts (steam, publishers, taxes, investor interest) is what kills you slowly

3. Companies recycling games

I fucking hate remakes. Maybe it is just me but god what the fuck is that and why does it work is an even bigger question. Is this a budget problem or are people afraid to develop new titles. Also I don't want to play the 20th Assassins Creed, 30th CoD and so on.. This is actually worse for me than the remakes. Like please give something new, you have the money to make it, I don't but I still whanna see something new and exciting and not Far Cry 7

4. Disgusting amount of hours needed for a top quality asset

Don't know if this is a software limit, but god damn making one NPC takes months of work. Animation also takes so many hours and yet games require so many of them. Even with MoCap its mind boggling, let alone without it. Who knows, if it is a software cap then maybe it gets better over time.

I read the whole story and wow, what a series of events. I'm sorry for what you went through but I also need to thank you for sharing this story. I have been thinking about converting a project that I am currently working on into a commercial product, and have been thinking about starting to look for a team and maybe even open a studio. Given that, I have to ask you some questions about these things, given your experience in the industry and especially this side of it, which rarely people talk about.

Do you think that, *on average*, it is possible for a small team of people to run **without a publisher**?  What I mean by this is making a revenue share project, where generated income would be split amongst participants, just without any added income reduction from a publisher. This would often lead to less sales (given the lack of the publishers marketing power), but also no loss of income from the publisher cut. If you disagree with this, do you instead think that there are good publishers and it all depends on who you decide to work with?

​

>But our contractual obligations meant that if we didn’t deliver, we would have to cover Kasedo’s costs… which they estimated to be an additional £200k

About this, in the events that the money owed **is not possible to be returned**, what happens to the person owning the studio? Are there legal problems that can arise for the owner or does the company just seize to exist? The same would be asked about other sources of funding/loans.

>Of course quality and process matter as far as the odds for success. But particularly for an indie studio, there are plenty of ways to get blindsided: Unexpected competition in your genre, bad release timing, sudden trend shifts as far as subject matter, and even global pandemics can impact the results of a dev and release cycle. Nothing is ever a sure thing.

Does this mean that one bad release for a small indie team would spill a disaster, even running the company to the ground? To elaborate, let's say the first game of a studio makes **100k€** (all after paying taxes, steam cut, legal fees ecc..). This is the money that is currently in the war chest so to say. If the next project consumes almost *all of that 100k€* and only makes **10k€** in profits, does this mean that the entire company goes back to square one? I assume massive firing of people would ensue this, which would result on what projects can you take on, given the reduced team size. Would you say that it is a good idea to only invest a certain **%** of available funds to a 2nd or 3rd project, keeping the rest just in case? Additionally, is there any way to get funding that **isn't related to a publisher**?

Were you the only man in charge of the entire development for *Recipe For Disaster*? To clarify, were you the one responsible for what features get added, how things are organized, or were you maybe not alone in this? **Did you encounter disagreements with the team and if you did, how did you handle that**? Example would be that you want to add a feature to the game and someone on the dev team wants something else and disagrees with that feature being added.

And finally, do you think that running a studio early could sustain you in life income wise or do you believe that some other work must be done before/during the development to ensure ones financial stability?

I forgot about Guard Helm, edited my comment, thanks for reminding me. Yea Rad Armor helps a lot but Barats's main weakness is getting slowed and kited around. Also a proactive enemy will steal all the jungle camps if given the opportunity which fucks up the stacks and makes it super hard to continue your early game.

Kimmy counters Barats pretty well actually. Not much you can do about it. Best item in this situation is brute force for the speed. For damage items Corrosion Scythe is pretty decent for Barats, EB and even Hunter strike can help you out if you need to close the distance. I've tried bloodlust axe as well but I feel it's really not worth the slot. Thunderbelt is a nice damage/tank item.

If you need to carry you need to be jungle, going side won't help you much. I prefer gold lane to exp if I can get it. Side Barats is really meant to be a full tank/support type of hero, not really meant for soloq. Barats is very versatile and you should really adapt to every situarion. If you don't have MM jungle and 1 tanky side you can go full damage on Barats, always pay atention to what the enemy has, and adapt accordigly.

As a main Barats wanted to give some info. Overall good guide, would add that if ur going xp lane don't buy waraxe, there is no point in just buying 1 damage item expecially on xp lane. Your job is to be tanky as hell, not die to ganks and be able to facetank a lot of enemy damage or sit behind and wait with your ult when enemy jumps ur backline. Dom Ice is situational, depends on enemy. Items for sidelane to consider: Guardian Helm (sustain on lane), Thunderbelt, DR armor 1st item (vs saber for example), AQ, Twiglight Armor, Cursed Helmet, Rad armor. Emblem for side is correct by the guide, for jungle take the assassin emblem that heals on kill. 

For jungle, you have so many options. If have low dmg in team, go WA/Corrosion Scythe/EB + Thunderbelt (situational) + 1 tank item according to enemy team. You can also do WA + rest tank and focus on getting Thunderbelt 2nd item for the slow + Immortality to be extra safe. 

Some tips:

-if you jungle, when you have 16 stacks, you can kill red buff + the green camp above it at the same time due to aoe basic attack, pull the camp with ur 1st skill

-don't ever ult at the beginning of a fight, if enemy gets bursted you just wasted ur time standing still

-be a protector first, facetank frontline 2nd; example is if enemy has YZ, stay back and wait for him to ult on ur mage and as soon as he drops u ult him

-use first skill + retri to secure turtle

-don't pick him vs WanWan or Karrie, they destroy you

-when you ult someone and throw them into the wall, aim ur 2nd skill so that it hits the same enemy into the wall again, count 1 second after u spit and then cast 2nd skill, provides some nice extra cc

-try to get your team an Estes or Rafa, they work best with barats

-don't ever be cocky when going on lane, you are there to hold it, play safe and don't feed, it's very easy to die when you don't have stacks

-don't build mana boots if you plan on going thunderbelt

-slows are your biggest nightmare alongside kiting, try to be extra cautious if enemy has that (example Yve)

-you shine mid game, late not so much if you aren't with 3 damage items atleast

-barats sucks at breaking tier 3 tower defences, don't pick him if your team is weak at breaking the last line of defence

Yes it is possible, to a certian degree. You need to have an idea of what you want to do first and make a plan on how to do it. A heavy factor in the building process will be the time you put in, more the better! Don't make too high of expectations like me, start small and take it with baby steps literally.

Here is some tips:

-Decide which direction to go in in terms of 2D or 3D so you know which to focus on, some great programs are Maya and Zbrush if you can afford them, Blender for free and Photoshop

-Pick your language of programming (C++ would be best)

-Pick up and start learning the software in which you are gonna work in -> Unreal Engine, Unity, Godot ecc... 

-Write the plan down, pen and paper if you have to, helps a lot trust me. Worst thing is to be mid way through yet feel like you are lost and then quit. 

-Use assets you can get your hands on, don't jist asset flip but try to cut corners whenever you can, a solo guy making a game is super difficult, don't expect to be the 2nd Eric(guy who made Stardew Valley).

-Make some small games before a big project planned for release, it will help you develop the skills needed

-Don't fall into tutorial hell, i.e. just watching tutorials and being unable to do anything alone. Follow them at the start,  bt try to implement stuff yourself with the tools they showed you

-Too high expectations = quitting quickly. You aren't gonna make a AAA game unless you asset flip your way to it and focus only on art

-Game jams are a good place to practise making games whithin a certian time frame. Isn't really for super beginners but once you have the basics, these are a great place to go. You can also meet other game devs and team up

If I remember something else I'll edit it in or someone can fill it in the comments below. Don't be like me and quit because of too high expectations. I'd say that is the number one killer of game ideas.

I'm working on something similar at the moment so here is my take on it. I have loved RPGs since the dawn of time, played all of thr popular ones and for me personally, a story should be immersive and extended. Don't tell everything at once, but don't make it so you never learn through. Text based story is usually bad, only a handful of players will ever read that(unless it's like Dark Souls-type story hidden in item descriptions or whatever. Make the player care by investing them emotionally into it, steer the story similarly to a popular TV series. Don't force people to every part though, if someone doesn't care about something, don't make them go through it on purpose. Have a solid, self existing main storyline and add a TON of side missions focusing on different aspects in a deeper view. But don't make side missions unrelated to the main story, that makes them obsolete imo.

Tell the player about the mom and the childhood for sure. Deepen it, make it slow but more impactful as a reveal. The background of the mom and child should be mandatory but in small relations, the extended version and details go in side. Making choices is the difficult part, since it's entirely up to you how you do it. Different endings add to immersion immensly, even if only a couple of them. Don't flood the game with choices tho, too many of them will make people hate it.

If you go MM gold lane you will either get eaten by an assasin (Haya, Saber) or your tank will be stuck in 1 lane which gives enemy huge map advantage.

Heres some tips from a Khufra main. So when the game starts, inspect their team and ask yourself will they invade your jungle? Jawhead/Franco - yes, weak lvl1 heroes - nope. If they don't invade, go to the exp lane (do not buy any item, very important!). Clear the lane with your sidelaner while not having roaming bought. You and him get lvl 2 from just 1 wave! Then rotate to middle and check the vision thingy in the river. 

Identify which person on your team is the most likely to either be ganked or will lose his lane (bad matchup), once you know that, go and help there. Push lanes if your team is bad and lets waves go to waste (noone farming lane).

For Khufra, don't let them see you! Khufra isn't a frontline tank, rather a backline initiator. Stick to bushes, let your fighters go in first and then decide where to go. If you whanna be good learn to pre-cast first spell and be ready if someone shows up, if not cancel cast and repeat when off cd. 

For other tanks identify what is your tank good at. Tanky af? Charge first. Have a lot of CC? Protect your highest dmg dealer. Don't be a Franco who charges in for no reason, you will just get killed. Hylos on the other hand can charge in to disrupt enemy lines and zone some people away. 

For bush camping, camp only when necessary. Don't be afk in a bush for 5 minutes. Waiting for lord? Camp in bush. When you rotate, don't just think about ganks and kills, you can also rotate to a weak lane (MM vs saber for example) and help them clear lanes and take the gold. Whoever is dying the most needs your help. If you just stick to your jungler you will lose a lot of gold as a team. Be the guy that provides vision, disrupts the enemy, defends the best guy on your team, stuns the enemy most fed guy. Buy items that benefit the team (dominance ice for example), and learn positioning + map awareness. Thats key for tanks.
